Nearly perfect - love it - highly recommend. Overall, I love Monarch Money! It does an excellent job of connecting to almost all my financial accounts and has become an invaluable tool for understanding and managing my household finances.

One of its greatest strengths is the ability to track spending across multiple accounts in one place. Instead of reviewing individual bank accounts and credit card statements, I can see where our money is going, identify spending patterns, compare expenses from month to month, and distinguish recurring expenses from occasional purchases. This makes it much easier to understand our actual cost of living, identify opportunities to save, and make informed financial decisions. I particularly appreciate being able to examine individual transactions rather than relying solely on broad spending categories.

I also love the ability to download transactions as CSV files. This allows me to conduct more detailed analysis in Excel, create customized reports, and track spending over longer periods. An option to automate or schedule these exports would make an already excellent feature even better.

The new email receipt system is a fantastic improvement, especially for tracking Apple purchases and subscriptions. Being able to connect receipts to transactions makes it much easier to understand charges that otherwise appear with vague merchant descriptions.

There are, however, a few areas that could be improved.

Account connectivity: Reauthorizing accounts that require two-factor authentication can be frustrating. I wish there were an easier, centralized process for identifying disconnected accounts and reconnecting them.

Duplicate accounts: When a retirement account becomes disconnected and is subsequently reconnected, it can be difficult to determine whether Monarch has created a duplicate. This raises concerns about the accuracy of account balances and net worth calculations. Better duplicate detection and a straightforward way to reconcile accounts without losing transaction history would be extremely helpful.

Transfers versus income: Monarch could do a better job distinguishing actual income and expenses from transfers between accounts. Internal transfers, credit card payments, and certain retirement transactions can distort income and spending reports when they are incorrectly categorized. Better automatic identification and reconciliation would significantly improve the reliability of its financial reporting.

Despite these issues, Monarch is an excellent product. It has given me a much clearer picture of our household finances and made tracking spending considerably easier. I especially appreciate that it provides both an accessible overview of our finances and the flexibility to conduct more detailed analysis when I want to dig deeper.

Monarch surfaces this data as “you owe $6,000 this month” and shows the monthly recurring dollar amount as something atrociously high.

Premium Price, Surprisingly Basic Problems. TL;DR: Monarch has some good ideas and is generally well designed, but for $15/month it gets several basic things wrong: the trial is too short, auto-categorization is unreliable, rule priority is opaque, and category/budget organization is unnecessarily confusing and restrictive.

Full Review:
Monarch is feature-rich and mostly well designed, but several fundamental blunders seriously degrade the experience and make me question how a $15/month, award-winning budgeting app can get some of the basics so wrong.

First, the 7-day free trial is far too short and feels greedy. This is a budgeting app built around monthly budgeting. You realistically need at least one full budgeting cycle to understand how transactions, rules, rollovers, recurring expenses, and actual spending behave over time. Seven days is barely enough to finish setting everything up, much less evaluate whether the product actually works for you.

Second, auto-categorization needs to be rock solid at this price, and it simply isn’t. Monarch categorized a Baskin-Robbins purchase as a coffee shop. Baskin-Robbins. One of the most recognizable ice cream chains in America. As a coffee shop. That is the budgeting-app equivalent of categorizing McDonald’s as a hot dog stand. Mistakes happen, sure, but errors this basic seriously undermine confidence in the system.

The rule system is unnecessarily opaque and inflexible. Rules apparently execute in top-to-bottom order, with the first overlapping rule winning, yet this hierarchy is not made clear in the UI. Worse, there is no way to reorder rules. If rule priority matters to the outcome, users need both a clear indication of that priority and direct control over it.

Category organization is another mess. Categories exist within groups, yet the settings UI presents groups and categories together in a flat list at essentially the same visual level, even though they are fundamentally different objects. Group ordering should be clearly separated from category ordering within each group. Reordering itself also seems buggy, with changes sometimes failing to persist, and it is unclear how the order configured there relates to the ordering shown in the Budget tab. This entire interaction needs a rethink.

Finally, Flexible budget items appear to be automatically ordered by spending level, with no obvious way to manually reorder the groups and categories. Why? A premium budgeting app should not be making an arbitrary presentation decision like this with no override. Fully unconstrained category and group ordering is a basic organizational feature, not an advanced request.

There is a lot to like about Monarch, which makes these shortcomings surprising and more frustrating. The app is close to being excellent, but at $15/month the standard should be much higher. Basic categorization accuracy, understandable rule precedence, reliable reordering, and full control over budget organization should already be solved problems.

Monarch Made Taxes & Biz Ops So Much Easier!. The other is the Create Rule feature that allows you to take a transaction and customize it to automatically have attributes you assign for all future transactions. Say you have a business expense for supplies every few months that you want to tag (label) as business-related and/or as a tax write-off - any time you make this purchase in the future it will now have those tags. You can also edit the merchant name to better match what it reflects and much more. 

Lastly I recently had to fill out 6 months of profit & loss forms for legal purposes and I used the new AI they’ve implemented to automatically gather the items I specified, itemize them, and give me totals so I could simply plug-in the numbers (after double checking them for accuracy, of course 😉). 

I know there’s a number of good financial budgeting apps out there right now, but I’m glad I decided to try Monarch and it’s been so helpful with taxes and other legal uses that I’ve decided to keep subscribing at $14.99/month. 

At times, I wish it were a little cheaper, but when you consider the real-life implications of financial organization (or lack thereof) and how the practicality of an app like this changes the game for those things, the value you get in return is worth a lot more than $14.99 a month.

Monarch, otoh, has to be trained to do this, account by account— and if the transfer transactions signatures change in the slightest, it forgets this training, and reverts to booking credit card payments received as income, and the corresponding checking account transactions as expenses, wrecking cash flow reporting. So I’m effectively back to Quicken 98 behavior, in 2026, with the added bonus that I pay annually for the privilege of having my financial data online to be mined. Reconsidering my options now.

I recommend this app to anyone I know that could use help with their budget.

Great but has room for growth. For visualizing and keeping track of everything it’s amazing. I do find some flaws of it, though that I think they could definitely improve.

Making rules and goal setting. These are honestly very cumbersome. You can only automatically track income for goals. You can’t auto track expenses. So for example, if I get my paycheck income on my checking account, I would have to attribute that income to my goal. But that’s not realistic because I would transfer that money to my savings account or my investment account. But you can’t link a transfer to a goal. You also can’t see transactions on investment accounts right now (it’s in beta but it doesn’t work). I also can’t make a rule for transfers accurately (they need to allow the rules to say “from account” and “to account” because just filtering “account” isn’t specific enough), nor can I set up my savings as an expense without having to manually input those expenses as a contribution to the goal. I hope this makes sense but basically TLDR transferring money is not a forte for this platform. I do like that it says transferring money doesn’t have to be tied to the budget so that’s helpful but I do wish there was some way to actually link the transfer information. I don’t want to think of a transfer from my checking to my credit card as an “expense” and then an “income”. It should just be a transfer that I can attribute to both accounts. Honestly, I’ve gotten rid of my goals because they just became too annoying to deal with and if you do a rule where you put a bunch of transactions linked to a goal, you cannot mass change it or revert it so you also have to manually fix it if you accidentally do that or just delete the goal. Basically what I am saying though is that saving money and tracking savings in your budget is not flushed out enough because now my savings I have to consider as an expense because I can’t accurately categorize transfers as a saving. If I could say “transfers from X account to Y account contribute to my goal” that would be great, but all it is is “transfers in X account”. I don’t want ALL of the transfers contributing to the goal. Sorry for the rant but it definitely is something that I think should be more fine tuned. Unless I am missing an entire functionality.
